name: Light King's Blue
lede: Light King's Blue is a soft, greyed sky blue from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, a lightened version of the pigment name King's Blue rather than a blue with its own separate history.

sections.title: A paled pigment name
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 atlas carries this tone on plate XXII, hue 47* [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary lists it simply as pale blue, without a block number in our source, 6.3 units from Ridgway's reading, its Munsell notation given as 3.5PB 7.2/4.1 [1].

Its closest neighbor in our library is [[light-columbia-blue]], about 2.7 units away, almost the same color, followed by [[light-grey-blue]], about 3.4 units off and more blue [2]. [[cloudy-blue]] and [[burn-blue]] sit a little further, about 3.8 to 4.7 units off [2]. "King's Blue" was itself an artists' pigment name; what the unmodified pigment owes its name to is undocumented here [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive matches this tone in 222 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.93 percent, as photographed, more common than 65 percent of the named colors tracked [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.2 percent of the 1,674 paintings from that decade, 1.4 times its museums' expected rate [3].

Inside a painting it most often hides, in 50 percent of its 145 clearly-ranked appearances, a rank computed within each canvas so varnish cannot fake it [3]. C. W. Eckersberg carries it most often by raw count, in 5 of his 50 works here, though no painter stands out once measured against their own museums' baseline [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and the match is a computed color reading, not a pigment identification [3].
